summary.text: For each Collatz step from \(m>1\) to \(p\), a residual code \(r\) at \(m\) is lifted to \(r+1\) when \(p\) is nonbranching, and to \(2r+1\) or \(2r+2\) at a branching \(p\) according as \(m\) is even or odd; the decoding rules then return exactly to \(m\) with residual code \(r\). Inducting along a finite Collatz trajectory from \(m\) to \(1\), starting with residual code \(0\), therefore constructs an encoding rooted at \(1\) whose decoded value is \(m\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T(x)=\begin{cases}
x/2,&x\text{ even},\\
3x+1,&x\text{ odd}
\end{cases}
\]
be the Collatz map, where division is integer division. We assume the Collatz conjecture in the form: for every positive integer \(m\), there is a nonnegative integer \(k\) such that \(T^k(m)=1\).

We first restate precisely the tree-decoding process that defines the sequence. Call an integer \(v\) a branching value if
\[
B(v):\qquad v>4\quad\text{and}\quad 6\mid v+2.
\]
For nonnegative integers \(r,v\), define \(F(r,v)\) recursively as follows. If \(r=0\), set
\[
F(0,v)=v.
\]
If \(r>0\), put \(s=r-1\). Then:

* if \(B(v)\) holds and \(s\) is even, set
  \[
  F(r,v)=F(s/2,2v);
  \]
* if \(B(v)\) holds and \(s\) is odd, set
  \[
  F(r,v)=F(\lfloor s/2\rfloor,(v-1)/3);
  \]
* if \(B(v)\) does not hold, set
  \[
  F(r,v)=F(s,2v).
  \]

In every recursive call the first argument is smaller, so this definition terminates. The sequence in the problem is
\[
a(n)=F(n,1).
\]
Thus \(F(r,v)\) describes the result of starting the decoding algorithm at a tree node of value \(v\), with residual code \(r\); the actual sequence starts at the root \(1\).

The key point is that one Collatz step can be reversed inside this decoding procedure while suitably changing the residual code.

**One-step encoding lemma.** Let \(m>1\), let \(q=T(m)\), and let \(r\ge 0\). Define a new residual code \(R\) by
\[
R=\begin{cases}
2r+1,&B(q)\text{ and }m\text{ is even},\\
2r+2,&B(q)\text{ and }m\text{ is odd},\\
r+1,&B(q)\text{ does not hold}.
\end{cases}
\]
Then
\[
F(R,q)=F(r,m).
\]

To prove this, split according to whether \(q\) is branching and according to the parity of \(m\).

First suppose \(B(q)\) and \(m\) is even. Then \(q=m/2\), and because \(m\) is even we have \(2q=m\). Here \(R=2r+1\), so after the decoder decrements \(R\), its new temporary residual value is \(2r\), which is even. Since the current value \(q\) is branching, the decoder therefore moves to the doubling child \(2q=m\) and replaces the residual value by
\[
(2r)/2=r.
\]
Consequently its remaining computation is exactly \(F(r,m)\), proving \(F(R,q)=F(r,m)\) in this case.

Next suppose \(B(q)\) and \(m\) is odd. Then
\[
q=3m+1,
\]
so \((q-1)/3=m\). Now \(R=2r+2\). After decrementing, the decoder sees \(2r+1\), which is odd. At the branching value \(q\), it therefore moves to the other child,
\[
(q-1)/3=m,
\]
and changes the residual code to
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{2r+1}{2}\right\rfloor=r.
\]
Again the rest of the computation is \(F(r,m)\).

Now suppose that \(B(q)\) does not hold and \(m\) is even. As before, \(q=m/2\) and hence \(2q=m\). In this case \(R=r+1\), so decrementing gives \(r\). Since \(q\) is not branching, the decoder follows its unique doubling child, whose value is \(2q=m\), without halving the residual code. Thus it continues as \(F(r,m)\), as required.

The only remaining apparent case is that \(B(q)\) does not hold and \(m\) is odd. This case is impossible when \(m>1\). Indeed, an odd integer \(m>1\) is at least \(3\), and then
\[
q=3m+1\ge 10>4.
\]
Furthermore, since \(m\) is odd, \(m+1\) is even, and
\[
q+2=3m+3=3(m+1)
\]
is divisible by \(6\). Hence \(B(q)\) does hold, a contradiction. This completes all cases of the one-step encoding lemma.

We now prove the main reachability statement needed for the theorem. For every \(k\ge 0\), we claim:

> If \(m>0\), \(r\ge 0\), and \(T^k(m)=1\), then there is a nonnegative integer \(N\) such that
> \[
> F(N,1)=F(r,m).
> \]

We prove this by induction on \(k\).

For \(k=0\), the equality \(T^0(m)=1\) simply says \(m=1\). Taking \(N=r\) gives
\[
F(N,1)=F(r,1)=F(r,m),
\]
as desired.

Suppose the assertion is known for \(k\), and assume
\[
T^{k+1}(m)=1

after starting with some positive \(m\). If \(m=1\), there is again nothing to reconstruct: taking \(N=r\) gives \(F(N,1)=F(r,m)\).

It remains to consider \(m\ne 1\). Since \(m>0\), this means \(m>1\). Put
\[
q=T(m).
\]
The number \(q\) is positive: if \(m\) is even, then \(m\ge2\) and \(q=m/2\ge1\); if \(m\) is odd, then \(q=3m+1>0\). Also, by the definition of iteration,
\[
T^k(q)=T^k(T(m))=T^{k+1}(m)=1.
\]
Define \(R\) from \(m,q,r\) exactly as in the one-step encoding lemma:
\[
R=\begin{cases}
2r+1,&B(q)\text{ and }m\text{ even},\\
2r+2,&B(q)\text{ and }m\text{ odd},\\
r+1,&\neg B(q).
\end{cases}
\]
Apply the induction hypothesis to the positive integer \(q\), with residual code \(R\). It supplies an \(N\ge0\) such that
\[
F(N,1)=F(R,q).
\]
The one-step encoding lemma gives
\[
F(R,q)=F(r,m).
\]
Combining these equalities yields
\[
F(N,1)=F(r,m),
\]
which completes the induction.

Finally, let \(m\) be any positive integer. By the assumed Collatz conjecture, choose \(k\ge0\) with
\[
T^k(m)=1.
\]
Apply the reachability statement just proved with residual code \(r=0\). There is an \(N\ge0\) such that
\[
F(N,1)=F(0,m).
\]
By the base clause in the definition of \(F\),
\[
F(0,m)=m.
\]
On the other hand, by definition \(F(N,1)=a(N)\). Therefore
\[
a(N)=m.
\]
Since \(m>0\) was arbitrary, every positive integer occurs among the values of the sequence \(a(n)\), assuming the Collatz conjecture.
